question: Three hours later, the patient is reassessed. Her right arm is put in an elevated position and physical examination of the extremity is performed. The examination reveals reduced capillary return and peripheral pallor. Pulse oximetry of her right index finger on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

analysis: The patient's symptoms of reduced capillary return, peripheral pallor, and low oxygen saturation (84%) in the right index finger suggest acute limb ischemia, which can lead to tissue necrosis if not addressed promptly. Among the options provided, performing a fasciotomy (option opa) is the most appropriate next step in management, as it is indicated in cases of compartment syndrome or severe ischemia to relieve pressure and restore blood flow. Amputation (option opb) is a last resort and not indicated at this stage. Skin grafting (option opc) is not relevant in this acute setting. Decreasing IV fluids (option opd) does not address the ischemia. Escharotomy (option ope) is typically used for burns and is not indicated here. Therefore, the best-supported option is to perform fasciotomy to prevent further tissue damage.
